source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can Recombination Displace Dominant Scientific Ideas?
finding: Core claim. Atypicality (A-index, distant co-cited journals) and disruption (D-index) capture different processes. Atypical work extends concepts into new topic areas. Disruptive work replaces a dominant idea inside its own topic. Hypothesis H1: A and D are negatively correlated.
numbers: 41 million articles 1965-2024 (abstract); OpenAlex base 49 million. Figure 3: 40,935,251 articles 1965-2020, mean D falls as A rises in every discipline, period and team-size panel (95% bootstrap CI). Exact correlation coefficient is not given in the text.
quote: Disruption, in contrast, signifies the replacement of a dominant idea within its own topic.
limits: Short preprint. Effect sizes are in figures only. Atypicality is the Uzzi z-score measure, oriented so that higher means more atypical. Observational. Direction conflicts with the same group's 2022 paper (see a10).
agent_relevance: Open mode: a distant mix of ideas is not the same as an attempt that replaces the leading rule. Treat them as two separate attempt types.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can Recombination Displace Dominant Scientific Ideas?
finding: Functional equivalence principle. Displacement happens when a new idea does the same intellectual job as the dominant one, but better. Recombination joins complementary distant parts, so it rarely replaces anything ('microwave TV' example). Cases: Turing 1937 replaced Goedel 1931; Barabasi-Albert 1999 replaced Erdos-Renyi.
numbers: Two hypotheses: H1 (A and D negative) and H2 (theories harder to displace than methods).
limits: Argument by example and verbal theory; no formal model. Example pairs are hand-picked.
agent_relevance: Selection idea: a candidate that competes for the same role as the current best answer is a displacement attempt; a candidate that joins far-apart parts is an extension attempt.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can Recombination Displace Dominant Scientific Ideas?
finding: LLM-measured topical similarity. An LLM scored topical similarity between a paper and its most-cited reference. Highly disruptive papers are topically close to that reference even after controls for field, citation count and time. Highly atypical papers have low topical similarity to their dominant references.
numbers: Numbers for the LLM similarity regression are not printed in the text; only the direction is stated. A related field-overlap test is in a07 (0.52 vs 0.014 chance).
limits: Which LLM was used for the similarity step is not stated in the text read. Shown qualitatively. LLM judgment is a proxy for topic overlap, not ground truth.
agent_relevance: An LLM can act as a cheap judge of 'same job as incumbent' vs 'new context'. Check the judge's sign on held-out labelled pairs (G3).

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can Recombination Displace Dominant Scientific Ideas?
finding: Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct zero-shot labelled each paper as 'theory' (conceptually different from its top reference) or 'method' (refinement or formalization). The token probability for 'theory' falls as the year gap between paper and reference grows. Conceptual advances come soon after their reference; refinements come later.
numbers: 50,147 highly cited disruptive (D>0) papers classified; Figure 4 uses 52,488 highly cited papers 1900-2020. Robust to few-shot prompts, reworded options, and a third 'others' option (all reported 'consistent').
quote: Given two papers--Paper A {title, abstract} and its reference Paper B {title, abstract}--is Paper A better considered as (1) a 'theory' innovation
limits: Only zero-shot LLM labels; no human validation numbers given. The theory-vs-method split is crude. Llama may know the famous example papers from training (contamination risk).
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of the displacement idea. An open model gives usable probabilities for 'new concept vs refinement'. Use the probabilities, not hard labels.

source: Li, Lin, Wu (2025) Can Recombination Displace Dominant Scientific Ideas?
finding: Hypothesis 2 as reported: methodological papers are on average more disruptive than theoretical papers, yet canonical theories stay dominant longer than canonical methods (harder to displace). Turing replaced Goedel quickly; Watts-Strogatz 1998 replaced Milgram 1967 only after more than 30 years.
numbers: Goedel 1931 to Turing 1937 is 6 years; Milgram 1967 to Watts and Strogatz 1998 is 31 years. No aggregate persistence numbers in the text read.
limits: Persistence analysis details are in figures not extractable from the PDF text; two anecdotes are not a test.
agent_relevance: Dominant rules may need much longer or stronger evidence to be replaced than methods; do not drop an incumbent after one failed check.

source: Lin, Li, Wu (2025) The Disruption Index Measures Displacement Between a Paper and its Most Cited Reference
finding: The D-index measures relative innovation: a paper's ability to displace its most-cited reference. D rewrites as d_p/(1+b_p): d_p is the local displacement (share citing only the paper minus share citing it with its references); b_p is the burden (most-cited reference citations divided by the paper's own). Reference citations follow Zipf's law.
numbers: Zipf fit a=1.89, b=0.60 on 1,000 papers (mean reference list 29); mean Cmax/Ctotal 0.40 observed vs 0.42 predicted. Median d_p about -0.2; median b_p 119, so 1/(1+b_p) is about 0.01. Only 1% of papers have b_p<1. Among 22 million papers with 10+ citations: 65% d_p<0, 32% d_p>0, 3% d_p=0. Of 42 million OpenAlex articles 1900-2020, 38% have D>0.
limits: Authors are the index's inventors (stake in defending it). Approximation assumes shared citations are small. Contested by Huang and Xie 2026 (a26).
agent_relevance: This is the formal model of 'replace the incumbent'. A displacement score needs a named incumbent; an agent can compute it per candidate against the current best answer.

source: Lin, Li, Wu (2025) The Disruption Index Measures Displacement Between a Paper and its Most Cited Reference
finding: Expert validation and field-overlap test. Experts nominated disruptive and consolidating papers; D agrees with them. Highly disruptive papers share a topic field with their most-cited reference far more often than chance, which supports same-question replacement, not random recombination.
numbers: Survey: 20 scholars, 190 responses. Mean D of nominated disruptive papers 0.21 (top 1%); consolidating -0.011 (bottom 13%); AUC 0.83. Field test: 49,077 papers with >100 citations and D>0.2; 0.52 share a field with their top reference vs 0.014 expected by chance (37 times).
limits: Tiny expert panel. 292-category taxonomy with about two fields per paper makes overlap easy. Authors' own data.
agent_relevance: Evidence that real breakthroughs are targeted, not random mixes. Supports a displacement operator aimed at one named incumbent.

source: Lin, Li, Wu (2025) The Disruption Index Measures Displacement Between a Paper and its Most Cited Reference
finding: Team-size replication dispute. Wu 2019 found small teams more disruptive. Petersen et al. (5-year window, Microsoft Academic) found a positive effect. Lin et al. reproduced the positive effect with a 5-year window, and the negative effect returns with longer windows, turning at about 10 years.
numbers: Cohorts 1995-2019 with windows of 1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 25 years (e.g. 47,129 papers from 2019; 536,463 from 2010; 226,358 from 1995). Regression sample 1.7 million papers (1-10 authors, 5-50 references, 10-1000 citations).
limits: Authors defend their own earlier result. Huang and Xie 2026 argue the sign is a reference-count artifact. Both can be partly true.
agent_relevance: Delayed credit: a displacing idea can look like a loser for ten years. A short evaluation window can hide the candidates open mode wants.

source: Lin, Li, Wu (2025) The Disruption Index Measures Displacement Between a Paper and its Most Cited Reference
finding: Replication of Park et al. decline: Holst et al. 2024 found the decline mostly disappears without zero-reference records; Lin et al. say Holst's dataset had about 3 times more zero-reference records because it mixed in book chapters; Park et al. 2025 reported robustness after excluding zero-reference items. In science most papers consolidate; in patents most displace.
numbers: Science: 62% of papers have D<=0. Patents: 62% D>0, 38% D<0. Released D values for 49 million OpenAlex articles 1800-2024.
limits: Second-hand description of a live dispute; Park et al. 2025 not opened.
agent_relevance: The base rate of displacement is low (about 1% have b_p<1). Expect most attempts to consolidate and budget for it.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022) New directions in science emerge from disconnection and discord
finding: Earlier paper by the same group with the opposite headline: atypical (novel) papers are about twice as likely to disrupt as conventional ones, but slowly (10 years or more).
numbers: MAG: 87,860,684 articles; 35,431,832 with citations and references. Highly novel papers disrupt 61% vs 36% for conventional. Typicality (median z) vs D: Pearson r = -0.05 (p<0.001), i.e. atypical goes with disruptive. Only 2.3% of papers highly atypical; fell from 3.9% (1970) to 1.4% (2000).
quote: Atypical papers are nearly two times more likely to disrupt science than conventional papers
limits: Very weak correlation (|r|=0.05). The 2025 paper (OpenAlex, different binning) reports the opposite sign; the two are not reconciled in the texts read. Differences: MAG vs OpenAlex, window, binned groups vs means.
agent_relevance: Do not assume atypical = disruptive or atypical != disruptive; the sign depends on measure, data and window. Test on your own task.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022) New directions in science emerge from disconnection and discord
finding: Atypicality and sleeping beauties. Atypical papers gain citations slowly, then catch up; their share of disruptive citations rises with time.
numbers: Sleeping Beauty Index vs atypicality r = 0.08 (log-log, p<0.001). Cohorts 1970 (87,475 papers), 1980 (176,826), 1990 (318,914), 2000 (591,653); t-test on 2018 disruptive-citation fraction, novel vs conventional: t = 23.85, 33.04, 52.78, 88.76 (all p<0.001). Atypicality effect stronger in computer science and engineering than in biology, chemistry, physics.
limits: Correlation, not causation. Stable fields (biology, chemistry, physics) show a weaker link.
agent_relevance: A short-horizon judge undervalues distant combinations. Scoring needs a delayed or repeated check, not only the first pass.

source: Lin, Evans, Wu (2022) New directions in science emerge from disconnection and discord
finding: Computational model of atypicality: Uzzi's journal-pair z-score is a pointwise-mutual-information quantity, so atypicality equals distance in a learned embedding space (skip-gram word2vec on journal co-citation).
numbers: Journal embeddings: 50 dimensions, window 10, 5 negative samples; 2,429 journals (1970) and 8,009 (2000). Pearson r = 0.74 between z-score and embedding inner product.
limits: Two training years only; r = 0.74 is far from identity. No test that embedding atypicality predicts disruption better.
agent_relevance: Atypicality can be computed as embedding distance between the parts combined. An LLM embedding of the ideas gives the same kind of score.

source: Uzzi, Mukherjee, Stringer, Jones (2013) Atypical combinations and scientific impact (Science 342)
finding: Founding atypicality study. Each pair of cited journals gets a z-score (observed co-citation vs shuffled-citation expectation). A paper has a conventionality (median z) and a novelty (10th percentile z). Papers that pair a conventional core with a small tail of atypical combinations are most likely to be highly cited.
numbers: Not opened (paywalled; 403 and PMC blocked). Definition and the conclusion are taken from the description in Lin, Evans, Wu 2022 (a10). Exact odds ratios and sample size NOT verified this session.
limits: Unverified here; secondary description only.
agent_relevance: Best bet is a mostly conventional core plus a small distant tail, not all-distant. Matches an agent mixing a standard method with one far transfer.

source: Funk, Owen-Smith (2017) A dynamic network measure of technological change (Management Science 63)
finding: Original CD index for patents: citing patents that cite the focal patent but none of its references count as disruptive; those that cite both count as consolidating.
numbers: Not opened (paywalled). Rule recorded as described in a06: D = (Ni - Nj)/(Ni + Nj + Nk).
limits: Unverified here.
agent_relevance: Disruption is observed from downstream behaviour, not from the paper's inputs.

source: Wu, Wang, Evans (2019) Large teams develop and small teams disrupt science and technology (Nature 566)
finding: Applied the D-index to papers, patents and software; reported that smaller teams disrupt more and large teams develop.
numbers: Not opened (Nature page redirects to login). Per Lin, Li, Wu 2025 arXiv 2502.00219 (read): 65 million papers, patents and software 1954-2014; 877 Nobel papers; 13 control checks; 38,000,470 authors in fixed-effect models.
limits: Disputed on window length (a08) and reference-count artifact (a26).
agent_relevance: Small-team, long-horizon work is where disruptive attempts concentrate; relevant to how many parallel attempts to keep.

source: Park, Leahey, Funk (2023) Papers and patents are becoming less disruptive over time (Nature 613)
finding: Reported a steep decline in CD5 across fields and patents, with falling diversity of cited work and falling atypicality.
numbers: Not opened (Nature behind login; PMC blocked). Scale per Holst et al.: about 45 million papers and 3.9 million patents.
limits: Strongly disputed (a17, a18, a19, a21).
agent_relevance: A measured decline in disruption can come from the metric, not from the world.

source: Holst, Algaba, Tori, Wenmackers, Ginis (2024) Dataset artefacts are the hidden drivers of the declining disruptiveness in science
finding: Failed replication of the Park et al. decline. Records with zero references have CD5=1 and were hidden by a plotting bug; their share falls over time and drives the decline. Random rewiring of citations also reproduces the decline.
numbers: SciSciNet 39,888,199 papers: 97% of CD5=1 papers and 78% of CD5=1 patents have zero references. Source documents of these records mostly do cite (93% of papers, 98% of patents in a 100-record check).
limits: Preprint; Park et al. later said their result survives excluding zero-reference items (reported in a09).
agent_relevance: Metric artifacts can look like real trends. Check a score on null or shuffled data before believing it (G3).

source: Petersen, Arroyave, Pammolli (2023/2024) The disruption index is biased by citation inflation
finding: Disruption (CD) falls mechanically as reference lists lengthen and as self-citation raises triadic closure ('citation inflation'), so cross-time comparisons and team-size correlations are unreliable. Deduction, regression and simulation; synthetic networks released.
numbers: Citations C(t) grow at gC = 0.033 + 0.018 = 0.051 per year, doubling every 13.6 years. 2024 version (arXiv 2406.15311, also read): PNAS vs PNAS Plus (N = 18,644 papers 2011-2015, 12.6% PNAS Plus): the whole difference in mean |CD5| tracks reference length; br = -0.0039 (p = 0.002, 95% CI -0.0055 to -0.0023); about 35% fall in CD from 20 years of rising density; team-size effect tiny and turns positive at 8+ authors. Sample 7,768,207 papers.
limits: Critique of the index, not of atypicality. The team-size model is contested by Lin et al. (a08).
agent_relevance: Any counting-based score must be normalised for list length (G5: length-normalise).

source: Bentley, Valverde, Borycz, Vidiella, Horne, Duran-Nebreda, O'Brien (2023) Is disruption decreasing, or is it accelerating?
finding: With a citation-weighted disruption index on Park et al.'s data, disruption stays near its neutral value for 50 years and rises slightly after 2000. The fall in unique words is expected in a growing corpus.
numbers: Publications grow about 4% per year for a century and about 5% per year since 1950. Effect sizes are in figures only.
limits: Preprint; alternative index; no atypicality analysis.
agent_relevance: Different definitions of disruption give opposite trends. Report variants.

source: Fang, Evans (2025) Generalization and the rise of system-level creativity in science
finding: New measures: foundation (F), extension (E), generalization (G) indices from how a paper is cited with its references or its citers. Most 'disruptive' citations are really generalization (cited alone in a distant context), not displacement inside the field. Atypicality measures how a paper is built; F/E/G measure how it is used.
numbers: D vs G r = 0.37, D vs F r = 0.05 (U-shaped), D vs E r = -0.37 (df = 23,448,429). 73.96% of disruptive citations are generalizational. Generalization papers: references 0.05 SD farther than average, title tokens 0.29 SD closer. Extension papers: references 0.35 SD closer. Foundation index fell 0.059 to 0.025 (-57.6%) 1950-1990; extension rose 0.536 to 0.762; generalization fell 0.405 to 0.214 then rose from the early 1990s. Correlations of atypicality or surprise with F/E/G are modest.
limits: Preprint by Evans, who co-authored the 2022 atypicality-disruption paper. Citation-pattern classification is a proxy for role.
agent_relevance: A third kind of attempt: compress a known idea so it transfers to a far domain. Distinct from distant recombination and from replacement.

source: Fang, Evans (2025) Generalization and the rise of system-level creativity in science (supplement on atypicality)
finding: Atypicality trend replication. Park et al. report falling atypicality; with a fixed venue-pair z-score benchmark average atypicality rises. Part of the decline came from recomputing z-scores per period. Awards: Nobel papers go with foundational work, not with high atypicality or disruption; semantic atypicality predicts other major awards in all tested domains.
numbers: Logistic regressions with controls for citations, references, 5-year period and domain, separately for Nobel and other awards. Disruption and reference atypicality: weak or insignificant for non-Nobel awards (Medicine positive). Semantic atypicality: positive and significant in all tested domains.
limits: Rare-event problem with few award papers. Fixed vs moving benchmark is a modelling choice.
agent_relevance: Atypicality depends on the reference baseline; a baseline that moves with the data hides novelty. Fix the baseline when comparing attempts.

source: Bornmann, Tekles (2020) Convergent validity of several indicators measuring disruptiveness with milestone assignments to physics papers by experts
finding: Validation against expert milestone lists from Physical Review Letters: the original DI1 was not the best; the variant DI5 did better. Indicators correlate differently with expert milestones.
numbers: PRL 1980-2002: 44,812 articles, 39 milestone. Via the Leibel and Bornmann review: DI1 average treatment effect 0.14959 after matching; DI5 and DEP better; DI5n and DI1n failed to separate milestone from control. Bittmann et al. 2022: 21,153 ordinary and 21 milestone papers.
limits: Few milestones; unbalanced; physics only. Effect numbers for DI5/DEP come second-hand.
agent_relevance: No single score is valid; prefer variants checked against expert labels.

source: Leibel, Bornmann (2024) What do we know about the disruption index in scientometrics? An overview of the literature
finding: Review. Novelty indices (Uzzi atypicality, Wang et al. unique combinations) look only at references; DI1 also uses citing papers, so it captures impact too. Novelty may be necessary for disruption but is not sufficient. Only some novelty types link to disruption: new methods positive, new theories and results negative (Leahey et al. 2023, Citation Classics); self-rated theoretical originality positive, methodological not (Shibayama and Wang 2020).
numbers: Convergent validity evidence is 'not entirely conclusive'; DI5 shows higher validity than DI1. Bornmann et al. 2020 data: 157,020 papers 2000-2016, 45 Poisson regressions on F1000 tags.
quote: Although novelty may be necessary for disruptiveness, it is not necessarily sufficient to make something disruptive
limits: Review by index critics; Leahey and Shibayama-Wang findings are second-hand.
agent_relevance: Disruption and novelty need different checks, and the two novelty studies conflict on which type helps.

source: Leibel, Bornmann (2024) Specification uncertainty: what the disruption index tells us about the (hidden) multiverse of bibliometric indicators
finding: Computing disruption involves many hidden choices (window, reference threshold, self-citations, variant). Different analysts could reach different results; authors urge multiverse-style reporting.
numbers: Cites Schweinsberg et al. 2021: 19 analysts, same data and question, broad range of results. No new numbers on disruption.
limits: Letter to the editor; no new test.
agent_relevance: Report the spread over reasonable setups, not one best run.

source: Liang, Jiang, Hou (2020) Same data may bring conflict results: a caution to use the disruptive index
finding: Using Nobel-winning articles 1900-2016, conclusions from DI depend on citation window length, discipline and year; not every paper with DI = 1 is a breakthrough.
numbers: Medicine, chemistry and physics Nobel articles vs benchmarks, median DI per year. No single headline number.
limits: Small study, Nobel only.
agent_relevance: The window is part of the measure.

source: Huang, Xie (2026) Large scientific teams are more, not less, disruptive
finding: Standard D falls mechanically with reference count; equalising reference-count distributions reverses the small-team advantage. A one-reference measure (1D, the average of pairwise D against single references) separates recognised breakthroughs better and shows disruption rising with team size.
numbers: 47,134,871 OpenAlex papers (5+ references, 1+ citation). 1D AUC 0.94-0.98 over six benchmark sets; D AUC 0.26-0.79 (Nobel 0.731 vs 1D 0.981; Turing 0.79; Lasker 0.60; Test of Time 0.55; Physical Review Milestones 0.40; Science Breakthrough of the Year below 0.5). Reference count alone AUC 0.31-0.65. About 85% of the observed decline survives randomization in null networks.
limits: Preprint v2 (27 Oct 2026). Answered by Lin et al. 2026 (a27).
agent_relevance: Per-incumbent scoring (one reference at a time) fits the schema: judge a candidate against one named incumbent, not a pooled list.

source: Lin, Yang, Wu (2026) Large teams consistently develop science
finding: Reply to Huang and Xie: oneD labels developmental Nobel work as disruptive and becomes sensitive to reference length itself; original D shows no systematic dependence on reference length; even controlling reference count, larger teams are more likely to produce strongly developmental work.
numbers: Nobel case (Davis et al., Bose-Einstein condensation): pairwise D with top reference Anderson et al. (over 5,000 citations) = -0.59; Bradley et al. = -0.04; Petrich et al. = +0.89; Adams et al. = +0.96; original D = -0.55. Nobel AUC: oneD 0.97, D 0.78, |D| 0.89. Under D, 107 papers (21%) of the Nobel set score negative.
limits: Authors defend their own index. AUC alone does not show meaning, they argue. Dispute unresolved as of Oct 2026.
agent_relevance: One paper can displace some references and consolidate others. Track displacement per incumbent, not one global label.

source: Kim, Kojaku, Ahn (2025) Uncovering simultaneous breakthroughs with a robust measure of disruptiveness
finding: D gives conflicting values for simultaneous discoveries. A continuous embedding-based disruptiveness measure (neural embedding of future context) separates Nobel papers from others better and finds 'twins' with similar future context.
numbers: No headline number extracted from the text read.
limits: Preprint; embedding-based; not tested against atypicality.
agent_relevance: An embedding of downstream use gives a model-based score without a citation graph; fits LLM embeddings.

source: Wei, Kang, Pan, Yang (2026) Identifying disruptive models in the open-source LLM community
finding: Applies the disruption idea to LLM model lineage. Model Disruption Index (MDI) on Hugging Face derivation links: most models consolidate, a few become new bases.
numbers: 2,556,240 models; 29,286 intermediate models scored; mean MDI = -0.53, main peak at -1.0; giant component 299,490 nodes (43.70% of the network). In-degree power-law exponent 1.92; LOWESS crosses zero near in-degree 149. Median MDI by size: -0.9636 (<1B), -0.9259 (1-10B), -0.8000 (>10B).
limits: Descriptive; metadata-only lineage; MDI inherits D's weaknesses.
agent_relevance: First use of the displace-vs-consolidate measure on LLMs themselves: strong path dependence, few replace the base model.

source: James (2025) Measuring the potential of scientific literature: a network-based approach to identifying paradigm-shifting research
finding: Single-author preprint tests D on Nobel papers in physics, chemistry and medicine against citation-matched controls; reports higher D for larger teams and for longer titles and denser jargon in abstracts.
numbers: Exact figures not extracted in the text read.
limits: Single author; strong wording ('conclusively'); conflicts with Wu et al. 2019 and Lin et al. 2026.
agent_relevance: Low-weight evidence; one more case where the team-size result flips with set-up.
